articles.title: Coachella 2027: Dua Lipa set to be first female British headliner
articles.summary: Tame Impala and SZA join the top of the bill for the US festival, which also features Madonna and Diljit Dosanjh.
articles.body:
Coachella has announced the line-up for its 2027 festival, with Dua Lipa set to be the first solo female British artist to headline.

The Training Season singer is top of Friday's bill for both weekends in April, with psych-rock band Tame Impala headlining the Saturday shows and US singer SZA closing out both Sundays.

The massive festival returns to the California desert on 9 to 11 and 16 to 18 April next year, with more than 100,000 fans expected to attend each day.

Madonna is also set to return to the festival after a surprise appearance alongside this year's headliner Sabrina Carpenter , 20 years on from her first Coachella set.

The Queen of Pop came back with Confessions II, her first album since 2019, earlier this year and had been rumoured to be headlining Glastonbury 2027 before organisers ruled that out.

Swedish pop star Zara Larsson and US singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers are also set to perform, as well as Diljit Dosanjh who returns after making history in 2023 by becoming the first Punjabi language singer to perform at the festival.

Blackpink's Jisoo, US star Kehlani, rock band Weezer and Dancing On My Own singer Robyn are also among the artists on the line-up.

The festival will mark a reunion for Dua Lipa and SZA after the pair both headlined Glastonbury in 2024.

During her Pyramid stage set, Dua, who earlier this year married could-be James Bond actor Callum Turner , also brought out Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker.

She becomes the first British woman to headline Coachella after Charli XCX performed on the main stage in 2025 before Green Day's headline slot.

During the success of her album Brat, the 365 singer made headlines after being pictured wearing a 'Miss Should Be Headliner' sash following her set.

Green Day appeared to respond with frontman Billie Joe Armstrong wearing a Brat baseball cap during their performance the following weekend.

Other UK artists on the 2027 line-up include EsDeeKid, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith.

Coachella is one of the most high-profile music festivals in the world thanks to its line-up and reputation for attracting a celebrity audience.

articles.title: Ewen Ferguson: Scottish golfer targets PGA Tour after injury woes
articles.summary: Ewen Ferguson believes he is capable of competing for a place on the PGA Tour and has set his sights on bigger achievements in 2027 after putting an injury-hit spell behind him.
articles.body:
Ewen Ferguson believes he is capable of competing for a place on the PGA Tour and has set his sights on bigger achievements in 2027 after putting an injury-hit spell behind him.

The three-time DP World Tour winner says improved fitness, greater strength and a more consistent scoring game have provided encouragement before this week's season finale in Dubai.

Ferguson, who is making his fifth consecutive appearance at the tournament, admits his putting has prevented him from turning a solid season into a stronger challenge for tournament victories. However, after working hard to address the problem, he is confident his opportunity will come.

"My game this year has been consistent," the 30-year-old said. "My scoring average is lower than any other year but I've just not probably putted as well to get myself right in the mix to win a tournament.

"That's been a bit disappointing but I've been working on it a lot and you just have to keep doing it. Hopefully, it comes at some point and I might just come at the right week at the right time at a big one."

Warren returns to main tour after three-year absence

After suffering a series of injuries, Ferguson spent the past four months working closely with gym coach Kenny McKenzie and is feeling stronger than he has for some time.

"That's totally gone, which has been great," he said. "I've had no real pain anywhere.

"I've been working hard in the gym, put on quite a bit of weight in the correct way and I'm hitting it a good bit further, which has been quite nice.

"I noticed that even last week playing with Jon Rahm and Tommy Fleetwood. I feel like I can keep up with them a lot of the time, which is a bit nicer."

The improved physical condition has allowed Ferguson to prepare more effectively, with the Scot also travelling with a physiotherapist for 15 weeks of the year.

He believes that consistency - and a calmer approach to the game - have been important factors in his progress.

"I feel like when I'm out there and I hit bad ones, I kind of know why and I don't panic," he explained.

"I'm probably a bit more flatlined now, which is probably a good thing for a golfer."

Ferguson also retains Ryder Cup hopes but recognises he needs some bigger results to improve his world ranking.

"I feel like I can compete," he said. "Whether I'm at that level of playing those tournaments week in, week out right now, I'm probably not there but I feel like I can be.

"I'd love to be on the PGA Tour at some point and get myself out there with Bob [MacIntyre] and Sandy [Scott]."

A big performance in Dubai could also boost his chances of securing a PGA Tour card, although Ferguson acknowledges he will probably need a second place or a victory to make that happen.

"It's definitely not beyond me but very difficult to do with the calibre of the field," he explained.

"I know the course really well and I've done well here in the past. I know I can contend if I'm playing well."

Ferguson also believes his experience of living in the Middle East has helped his development as a golfer.

Having initially found the longer, more demanding courses in the region daunting, he has learned the importance of course management and playing to the conditions.

Calum Hill and Grant Forrest are the other two Scots in the field this week and Ferguson is delighted Marc Warren will be back competing on the DP World Tour after earning his place via the second-tier Challenge Tour.

"I'm looking forward to having Marc back out," Ferguson added.

"We all know he's an incredible golfer. He's got one of the best swings on tour and when he gets hot, he's something else. It's pretty cool."

articles.standfirst: Excelente comportamiento del golf español en la Escuela Europea que copa tres de las cuatro primeras posiciones
articles.summary: Excelente comportamiento del golf español en la Escuela Europea que copa tres de las cuatro primeras posiciones
articles.body: El golf español abrochó el miércoles tres tarjetas de las 15 disponibles en la Escuela de clasificación del DP World Tour, la promoción para seguir disfrutando de la condición de miembro de la máxima categoría europea. Josele Ballester, Rocco Repetto e Ivan Cantero coparon tres de las cuatro primeras posiciones en el Infinitum Golf de Tarragona tras seis jornadas de juego. Pablo Larrazábal, tras 19 temporadas en el European Tour de toda la vida, no pudo recuperar la membresía. Es la baja más sensible de una competición que es un test terrorífico. Ballester y Repetto, ambos de 23 años, acabaron en lo más alto con 32 golpes bajo par tras una ronda final de 65. A Josele, incluso, le cupo un doble bogey en la tarjeta del último día. El de Castellón, tras el fiasco del desenlace del LIV Golf, ha recorrido un largo camino. Se tuvo que inscribir en la primera fase y logró los suficientes puntos para saltarse la segunda e ir directamente a la final. (Resultados) El malagueño, por su parte, se ha significado este curso como un golfista experto en desenlaces bajo presión. Se estrenó este año en los grandes tras clasificarse por las previas para el US Open y ahora ha vuelto a rendir. En dos temporadas ha pasado de jugar el Alps Tour, la tercera categoría, a repetir dos campañas seguidas en la gran liga de este lado del Atlántico. En la jornada final embocó dos eagles -ha hecho cinco en seis días- que paliaron los cuatro bogeys que cosechó. Cantero, mientras, retuvo la tarjeta por tercera año a través de un torneo del que ya había salido airoso en 2019, el primer curso en el que saboreó efímeramente el DP World Tour. Ha tenido un curso paupérrimo, falto de confianza, apenas un decimoséptimo puesto en el Estrella Damm barcelonés, pero en la Escuela lo ha bordado con seis tarjetas por debajo de 70, en especial la del lunes cuando firmó 61 golpes, la mejor vuelta (igualada por otros) de todas cuantas se han jugado estos días. A expensas de las negociaciones de Jon Rahm con el PGA Tour y si a Chacarra -que pretende combinar los circuitos- le van a acompañar algún golfista más a la aventura americana, el golf español podría contar la próxima temporada con 14 jugadores: Eugenio, Sergio García, Ángel Ayora*, Ángel Hidalgo*, Nacho Elvira*, David Puig*, Jorge Campillo*, Manuel Elvira*, Alejandro del Rey, Rafa Cabrera, Pablo Ereño y los tres golfistas que sacaron el billete el miércoles. Entre los ilustres que sacaron el billete para la próxima temporada están el coreano Byeong Hun An, otro ex jugador del LIV; Tom Lewis y Edoardo Molinari. *Jugadores que aún pueden ganar la tarjeta del PGA Tour

articles.title: Some Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms
articles.summary: There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field will be given the green light.
articles.body:
Some Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments.

There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective".

But in a sign of the division within the party, more than a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns in Parliament about approving it. Others expressed support, pointing to economic benefits.

Supportive Labour MPs said some other parts of the world emitted far more greenhouse gases than the UK and warned of relying on imports. Reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.

Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support.

One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate".

"The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said.

Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer.

Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test.

"It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices."

Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise."

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

The UK government has always insisted that Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision, formally resting with Fahnbulleh . She green-lit production in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea last month, but Rosebank hangs in the balance.

Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields".

Licences for both Jackdaw and Rosebank were granted by the then Conservative UK government in 2022 and 2023 respectively.

But the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approvals unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a fresh decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch sought to tease at Labour divisions on the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday.

During the debate, Labour MP Anna Gelderd said: "We live in an unprecedented era where our energy security is more vital than ever, in which jobs and wealth must be protected and economic opportunities seized - on both of these points, Rosebank fails."

Labour MP Julia Buckley said she had received opposition to Rosebank from her constituents in "regularly flooded Shrewsbury" and said fossil fuels "belong in the past, not the future".

She urged Fahnbulleh to "reject the oil licence in favour of renewables", adding: "Please don't add further to our climate emergency."

Other Labour MPs expressed their support, including recently departed veterans minister Al Carns, who warned that Britain would continue to need fossil fuels for decades and importing more would be a mistake.

"Refusing to produce it here does nothing on its own to eliminate that demand - it simply increases our reliance on imports which can carry their own environmental cost," he added.

Those representing communities with ties to the oil and gas industry, including Jonathan Brash, the Labour MP for Hartlepool, stressed the benefits of approving Rosebank for British jobs.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Labour MP Bill Esterson, chair of Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, said "the economics of it (Rosebank) are that you should carry on with it" and "there's an element of energy security" by approving it.

Energy minister Michael Shanks told the debate the government would take a "pragmatic approach" to a clean energy transition, stressing it was "not a turn off the taps government, but nor can we justifiably be a drill every last drop government either".

"This government will not make decisions for this country which are not compatible with our climate obligations," he added.

articles.title: DP World Tour Qualifying School: England’s Tom Lewis and Ben Schmidt and Scotland’s Ryan Lumsden earn tour cards
articles.summary: The final stage of DP World Tour Q-School sees 20 players earn tour cards for 2027; Among them are England's Tom Lewis and Ben Schmidt, Scotland's Ryan Lumsden, and experienced Italian Edoardo Molinari; watch DP World Tour Championship live on Sky from Thursday
articles.body:
England's Lewis, who secured his place in the field by winning a play-off at the second stage earlier this month to earn alternate status, finished tied for fourth alongside Ivan Cantero.

Scotland's Lumsden carded a third 68 of the week over the lakes course to earn his DP World Tour card for the first time, and England's Schmidt earned his playing rights for the second time in three years.

Spaniards Jose Luis Ballester and Rocco Repetto Taylor shared victory at the final stage of DP World Tour Qualifying School.

Seven players - Cameron John, Dabid Nyfjall, Lumsden, Paul Beauvy, Jansen Preston, Philipp Katich and Matteo Cristoni - will be DP World Tour rookies in the 2027 season.

Molinari is the oldest of the class of 2026 graduates at 45, with France's Paul Beauvy the youngest at 23.

Germany's Philipp Katich shot a bogey-free 62 and only made Monday's 72-hole cut on the number.

"I really didn't think I had a chance today," said Katich.

"I actually can't believe it. It was a big goal of mine to play in Australia [at the start of the season], now I can play the whole season on the DP World Tour which is even better."

articles.title: The Annika: Nelly Korda seeks LPGA Hall of Fame place and familiar success at Pelican Golf Club live on Sky Sports
articles.summary: Nelly Korda and Charley Hull speak to media ahead of start of LPGA Tour's The Annika at Pelican Golf Club; Korda seeking fourth title at event and LPGA Hall of Fame place; Watch The Annika on LPGA Tour from 4pm on Thursday, live on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
Korda will make her first competitive start on the LPGA Tour since the FM Championship in August, and first appearance since the Solheim Cup in September.

The 28-year-old is already a three-time winner in her six prior starts at The Annika driven by Gainbridge at Pelican Golf Club, and is chasing her fifth win of the season.

"Eight weeks - I don't remember the last time I took that long off," said Korda.

"It was nice but by the middle of it I was ready to get going. There is only so many hours you can go out and practise and beat balls.

"I'm very excited to be back. I think it's more the rejuvenation of being really motivated to come back out, and sometimes when you play a lot and you travel a lot, you start to get a little stagnant.

"I'm not saying you're not driven but you just get a little tired, a little worn out, your body gets a little drained.

"When you do take that time to have a little bit of time for yourself to re-energise your batteries, you're very motivated to come back and play against the best players in the world and test yourself.

"I wanted to give my body a little bit of a break. It wasn't feeling too great. Last time I put myself into that position I ended up injuring myself and was out longer, so I would say that as I gotten older I've learned to listen to my body.

"Sometimes I just have to take that break. A lot of people may not agree with it. I have to really listen to myself and know what's best for myself."

Korda recently clinched her second player the year award after another year of excellence.

"Obviously it's not just me but it's my entire team behind me. I'm the one hitting the shots and grinding, but there is so much that goes on behind the scenes.

"I'm very grateful and also so thankful for everyone that has been with me through the ups and downs.

"Winning it in 2024 and having a little bit of an off year in 2025 and getting back to it in 2026, to me that's a testament of the people that I have behind me through the ups and downs just lift me up.

"I'm honoured and hopefully that continues to push me forward."

Britain's Charley Hull has played well at Pelican Golf Club with top-five finishes the past two seasons, including a runner-up finish behind Korda in 2024.

"I just had one week at home after Malaysia [Maybank Championship] and I was pretty much in bed by 6pm every day," Hull said on Wednesday.

"The jet lag got the best of me. The weather has gone foggy and cold at home but I love that kind of weather, so we've just been playing nine holes and just prepping as much as I can for these two weeks.

"These are my favourite two weeks of the year.

"It would be nice to get a win. Obviously I've won round the golf course next week back in 2016 and come second here, so hopefully I can get it going because I like the two weeks.

"I just need to hole some putts. I played so well in Malaysia but didn't putt that well. Still resulted in a top-10 finish but if I just get the putts rolling it should be a good week.

"I just need to go out there and have fun. Play a bit of golf and enjoy it. Win or lose on a Saturday, Sunday."

articles.title: How climate change is affecting children's wellbeing after record summer
articles.summary: With a record summer this year in the UK, many people may be feeling anxious about climate change.
articles.body:
Millions of children across the UK say climate change is impacting their wellbeing after relentless heatwaves, wildfires and flooding.

Teenagers have said this year's extreme heat has left them feeling "powerless" and "hopeless" for the future, with experts explaining that climate anxiety is a sense of fear and worry linked to the changing climate.

Rebecca Fulford, 21, from Gloucestershire, said: "Often it feels like young people have the most expectation on them to take action. However they also have the least power."

Professor Dan O'Hare from Bristol University urged parents to validate the emotions of children who are dealing with climate anxiety, warning it can leave them feeling isolated.

Nearly two-thirds of secondary school children (about 3.4 to 3.6 million pupils) experience mental health symptoms linked to environmental concern, according to the British Science Association.

Elsie Brewer, 18, and Dylan Martch-Harry, 21, both from Wiltshire, said they have experienced climate anxiety first hand as a result of 2026's hottest summer on record and reading news headlines.

Brewer said that she sometimes feels "powerless", questioning what she can do that will make a change.

"But then at the same time if I just ignore it and forget about it so that I don't get anxious about it, nothing will change," she added.

Martch-Harry studied environmental science at university, where he said he was exposed to the realities of climate change that his peers are unaware of.

This includes devastating floods in Pakistan in 2022 when about a third of the country was submerged.

Martch-Harry said we need to all "do our part" by volunteering or thinking before buying things and doing certain activities.

He said: "Within this country we are very sheltered to the impacts of climate change, a lot of people I know just don't really know the overall impact that's happening globally."

While Brewer believes community action is important, she said that real change can be made with more large-scale decisions on climate change by the government.

Lauren Dicken, a community engagement assistant from Bath, who works at the youth-led environmental and educational charity Another Way, describes climate anxiety as a "rational" response that is experienced differently by various people.

Dicken has a chronic illness which she said is exacerbated by heat, making this summer's heatwaves challenging for her.

"I think it was the first time for a lot of people [where] they were like, "Oh it's here and it's real and it's affecting me and people I care about and vulnerable people and people all across the UK'," she said.

Dicken works with numerous young people raising awareness about climate change and hosts monthly drop-in sessions where people with climate anxiety can talk about their feelings.

"Knowing that you're part of the solution in some ways [rather] than part of the problem really helps me," she said.

Educational psychologist Dan O'Hare from the University of Bristol said he believed climate anxiety is not limited to emotions of concern.

He said: "It might be anxiety and worry, but it might also be anger and rage.

"You cannot separate the physical and the psychological, the physical experience of our changing climate affects our psychological state as well," he added.

Mental Health UK, a charity promoting positive wellbeing, suggest getting involved with youth action small groups is one way for young people to feel more at ease.

The Great Big Climate Circus, run by Creative Sustainability based in Gloucestershire, is a project aimed at helping young people reconnect with nature in a fun way.

According to statistics from the Woodland Trust, almost one in three people aged 16-24 (33%) are scared when hearing about climate change.

Honour Binning, the project manager at Creative Sustainability, said the group avoid focusing on climate "doom and gloom", as many young people reported facing climate anxiety already.

Leo, who also attends the group, said: "The most worrying part of climate change is the food and water shortages."

He said that "clear, sustained evidenced-action with clear impacts" will help young people to feel less anxious.

"I am very new to this group, but I am very hopeful, from meeting like-minded activists to help cause change which makes me more hopeful," he added.

Adam Gain, activities lead at Creative Sustainability, said children being exposed to climate anxiety during their formative years can have a "detrimental" impact.

He said: "There's a lack of climate education."

"It's really hard to balance feeding people the honest truth and the facts and mitigating against the mental health impact of that as well," Gain added.

Fulford, who is also part of the climate group, said: "From the responses we have collected at events, it is clear that young people want to see an increase in the education they receive on the climate crisis and direct engagement from local and national leaders."

Professor Myles-Jay Linton advised climate-anxious people to find a community of people feel the same way.

He recommended, "joining community groups and local initiatives where you can identify other people who recognise this as a challenge and then come up with joint action so that [it] does not feel so overwhelming."

Lizzie Testani from Bristol Climate and Nature Partnership, a network aiming to steer Bristol towards being net-zero, said people should focus on what they can do and what they are already doing.

Testani said: "Find out what else is happening and look for the types of things that feel a part of the solution. Think about and prioritise how you can stay well - your wellbeing is really important."

The company hold monthly 'Green Mingling' sessions where people across the city can come together and share ideas around maintaining a healthy climate.

articles.title: Victorian gasworks in Bradford turned into heat pump network
articles.summary: The Bradford Heat Network on Thornton Road is heating City Hall, the courts and the university.
articles.body:
A Victorian gasworks has been turned into a £75m heat pump network that will supply warmth to courts, council buildings, a university and a college.

The Bradford Heat Network, in Thornton Road, which began operating earlier, uses air source heat pumps to warm water, which is then run through underground pipes to customers.

Developed by low-carbon heat network developer 1Energy, the project will eventually use waste heat from a planned 5.6-megawatt data centre on Thornton Road, and is expected to cut carbon emissions for the companies that use it by at least 75%.

John Hartley, CEO of 1Energy, said the project would put Bradford at the forefront of modern energy infrastructure.

"This is one of the biggest air source heat pumps in the UK and it is state of the art in terms of its efficiency model," he said.

"It's able to serve historic buildings and new builds. So one of our first customers was the City Hall and we're talking to people who are building new developments."

At the site engineers are able to generate and store heat, meaning it can be discharged "when they city needs it", he explained.

"It allows us to control when we generate heat based on when the prices are low, when the carbon impact is low, and that's a way of Bradford centralising and taking control of its own heat production."

Bradford City Hall, the courts building, the University of Bradford and Bradford College are among the sites that will use the network, which carries heat across Bradford via a 5km (3 mile) network of underground insulated pipes.

According to 1Energy, the project can also incorporate additional local heat sources as it grows, such as surplus heat from businesses.

Explaining how the network will recycle heat from the planned data centre, Hartley said: "Data centres generate lots of heat they have to get rid of and that for them is a cost.

"We can take that heat for free – which helps them because they get rid of that cost – and it helps us lower our cost of production", he said.

Operations director Bhavya Patel said it was a great example of how data centres and heat networks "can deliver a sustainable future for a city".

"There's a real opportunity here from Bradford's perspective because the waste heat, rather than being rejected up in the air, can be directly taken up by the neighbouring heating plant room and hence the sustainability impact is really high," he said.

The project has been funded with £55m of private capital and £20m of government investment through the Green Heat Network Fund (GHNF).

A further £9.7m in GHNF funding has been secured to expand the network.

Deputy leader of Bradford Council Andrew Judson said the plans strengthened the city's offer to businesses and developers.

"It is an achievement the whole city can be proud of, showing how Bradford is leading the way in building a more resilient local economy.

"By reducing reliance on imported gas and improving air quality, the network will bring lasting benefits for local people.

"As it grows, it can support more businesses and buildings, providing infrastructure that helps Bradford attract further investment and thrive."

articles.title: Cardiff data centre near Llanrumney called in by Welsh government
articles.summary: The planning minister took the decision the evening before a council meeting to discuss the proposal.
articles.body:
Controversial plans to build a data centre in Cardiff will be decided by the Welsh government rather than the city's council.

Developer Curtis Hall wants to build the 30,292 square-metre facility on the site of a park and ride near Llanrumney in the capital's eastern suburbs, and is seeking permission for gas turbines that could temporarily power the site.

Officials said "substantial controversy" meant it should be determined by the Welsh government.

The decision was made by Welsh Planning Minister Sian Gwenllian the evening before a meeting where councillors had been due to discuss the scheme .

Curtis Hall said it is committed to engaging with ministers on the scheme.

The decision means a planning inspector will examine the application, before the planning minister makes a decision.

A public inquiry is one of the options the inspector could take. No timescale for when the decision has been issued has been published.

Some campaigners protesting on the Senedd steps on Thursday welcomed the move to take the planning application away from Cardiff council, whose officers had recommended councillors give their approval.

The Welsh government could chose to approve the application, however.

It comes as the Welsh government develops its own national policy on data centres, and after some party backbenchers including a minister had complained about the Cardiff plan.

Curtis Hall's application attracted petitions with about 4,000 signatures, and formal objections from all of Caerdydd Fynnon Taf's Members of the Senedd.

Concerns have ranged from the site's climate change impact to the loss of the park and ride service, air quality, lighting, noise, flood risk and water use.

According to the letter to Cardiff Council, Gwenllian "concluded the proposed development raises issues of more than local importance, including potential conflict with national policy on transport, energy and flood risk".

Setting out her reasons, the letter said: "Wide interest in the environmental impact and the policy in relation to data centres means the case has generated substantial controversy beyond the immediate locality."

The decision comes months before the May's local

Curtis Hall's application had attracted opposition from all the constituency's Plaid, Labour, Reform and Green Members of the Senedd , including a Welsh government minister.

Jo Stevens, Labour MP for Cardiff East, had told residents she had given the plans "conditional support" on the basis it did not compromise local water supplies.

She said the case for data centres "of this type reflects the evidenced demand for digital infrastructure to support the UK's growing technology sector".

Plaid Cymru MS Nick Carter, who was among those who requested the call-in, said the move was the "right decision and a major step forward for everyone who has fought to protect this community".

Local campaigners and politicians had requested the call-in in part because they believed the issue should be a matter of national policy, rather than dealt with by councils.

Reform MS Cai Parry-Jones had objected but argued the Welsh government should not have called the project in.

He said: "My constituents are the ones who would live with the loss of the park and ride, or benefit from the investment a data centre might bring.

"It should be their elected councillors, acting on their behalf, who decide whether this project goes ahead, not the Cardiff Bay lanyardocracy."

The decision led to the cancellation of a meeting of Cardiff's planning committee on Thursday, and a planned protest moved from County Hall in Cardiff Bay to the Senedd steps.

Abi Baxter, secretary of campaigning union Acorn Cardiff, said the group - which has been involved in protests against the scheme - was happy with the decision.

"It was going to replace the Llanrumney Park and Ride - that would have left residents without transport."

She acknowledged that the "fight" was not over, given the Welsh government could give it the go-ahead.

"We don't know what the Welsh government will do, absolutely. But let's hope that they listen to the community."

Friends of the Earth called the proposal to potentially use 49.9MW gas turbines for up to five years to power the site until a grid connection can be obtained as "climate-wrecking".

The developer said it would only be used in a worst-case scenario if other technologies could not be deployed.

Energy generation facilities of 50MW need planning permission from the Welsh government. Curtis Hall denied it was trying to avoid having to make such an application by limiting the plant to 49.9MW.

Cardiff Council planners had recommended councillors give the data centre the go-ahead, helping to diversify the capital's economy and provide a new transport link into Llanrumney.

The council had said that many of the impacts of the site could be avoided, mitigated, compensated for or appropriately managed - and that air quality effects were not considered significant.

It recommended that the planners enter an agreement to ensure an alternative park and ride with no fewer than 225 spaces, with the same number of spaces kept at the facility until the alternative site is completed.

The council's planning committee had been due to discuss the plans on Thursday before the meeting was cancelled.

Confirming the call-in, a Welsh government spokeswoman said: "This case will now be passed to Planning and Environment Decisions Wales [PEDW] who will examine Cardiff Council's planning application and provide a report to the cabinet minister for local government, housing and planning to make a final decision in due course."

A spokesperson for Curtis Hall said: "We remain committed to engaging constructively with Welsh government, Cardiff Council and the local community, and hope to realise the opportunities this investment could bring, subject to Welsh government enabling this project to move forward."

articles.title: Funding blow puts Star of Caledonia landmark artwork in doubt
articles.summary: The Star of Caledonia needs a "Christmas miracle" after a major funder pulled out leaving it needing £8m.
articles.body:
Plans for a landmark artwork at the Scotland-England border have been put on hold after a major funder withdrew support.

An emergency board meeting of the Star of Caledonia Trust (SCT) has agreed to pause the scheme near Gretna Green until spring next year while it looks to fill a funding gap of £8m.

It has now launched an urgent Save Our Star campaign in a bid to ensure the scheme - which hoped to attract 200,000 visitors a year - can go ahead.

Lucy Houston, who chairs the SCT, said: "This is a setback, but it is not the end of the Star."

Scotland-England border artwork plans approved

Original or truly awful? Scotland-England border artwork divides opinion

The story of the multi-million pound project goes back a quarter of a century, with a bid to create a landmark like the Angel of the North in the wake of the foot-and-mouth outbreak of 2001.

Various planning and financial setbacks have hit the scheme down the years and the design - by Cecil Balmond - was reduced in height.

Opinion is split about the artwork, with some describing it as "original" but others saying it is "truly awful".

It was hoped it could be completed by next year but - without full funding in place - it now faces an uncertain future once again.

Houston appealed for people to come forward if they are keen to see it progress.

"The project has come so far, and the support from our partners and the community has been incredible," she said.

"This Christmas, we are hoping for a Star of Caledonia miracle.

"Whether it's one major donor or several supporters joining together, we would love to hear from anyone who shares our vision and could help us cross the finishing line."

She told the BBC it was "disappointing" news, but they remained closer than they had ever been to building the landmark.

"We've had the costings in and we've worked really hard to bring them to within budget," she said.

"But the economic climate has changed and significant private donation is no longer available to us.

"So the trust has decided to pause the project until spring 2027 whilst we look for new funding."

Planning approval remains in place. with the last conditions in the process of being met.

She said the trust remained "optimistic" despite the latest setback, and said they remained in dialogue with the funder who had dropped out of the project.

Renewable energy company CWP Energy has previously been named as a major supporter of the plans.

The BBC has approached the firm to ask if it remains committed to the scheme.

articles.title: DP World Tour Championship: Rory McIlroy boosts Race to Dubai hopes as Joost Luiten grabs shock early lead
articles.summary: Joost Luiten holds a one-shot lead over Jacob Skov Olesen at the DP World Tour Championship; Rory McIlroy in tied third as he looks to overtake Eugenio Chacarra in the Race to Dubai standings; watch live on Friday from 7am on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
McIlroy, who needs to finish fourth or better to have a chance of surpassing Eugenio Chacarra in the season-long standings and win the Race to Dubai for an eighth time, carded an opening-round 69 at Jumeirah Golf Estates.

The world No 2 mixed five birdies with two bogeys in breezy conditions on the Earth Course, where he missed an eagle opportunity at the par-five last that would have moved him above Chacarra in the projected Race to Dubai standings.

McIlroy sits in tied-third on three under and within two shots of Luiten, the last player in the field and 56th in the season rankings, who jumped top of the leaderboard after a five-under 67.

Jacob Skov Olesen briefly shared the lead but is one behind Luiten on four under, with Victor Perez, Gregorio De Leo, Freddy Schott and Francesco Laporta all two back alongside McIlroy, while Race to Dubai leader Chacarra opened with a level-par 72.

McIlroy can guarantee Race to Dubai victory by winning this event for a fourth time, with The Masters champion making the dream start by rolling in an eight-foot birdie at the first.

He responded to a three-putt par at the second by birdieing the par-three fourth, then bounced back from a sloppy three-putt from 15 feet at the fifth by taking advantage of the par-five seventh.

Chacarra was over-par until his three-birdie run from the seventh, seeing both reach the turn in 34, before McIlroy holed a birdie from the fringe to briefly get within two of the lead.

The leading pair in the Race to Dubai stumbled slightly over the closing stretch, with Chacarra making two bogeys in three holes from the 13th and McIlroy dropping a shot at the par-five 14th after missing the green with his third shot.

McIlroy hit a glorious approach to within 15 feet at the par-five last to leave a late eagle look, which would have seen him leapfrog Chacarra, although he had to settle for a two-putt birdie after leaving his effort short.

Luiten was in the first pair out on the opening morning and raced to the top of the leaderboard with a front-nine 31, then cancelled out back-to-back bogeys from the 11th by birdieing the 13th and 18th to reclaim top spot.

Olesen is also among those looking to secure PGA Tour membership - available to the top 10 eligible players in the Race to Dubai rankings, with the Dane's final-hole birdie getting him within one of Luiten, on a day where only 22 of the 50-man field finished under-par.

McIlroy was among nine players starting the week with a mathematical chance of topping the Race to Dubai rankings, but Jon Rahm and Daniel Hillier - who both carded one-under 71s - the only others to break par on the opening day.

Casey Jarvis, Jayden Schaper and Ryan Fox - who need a victory to have any chance of claiming No 1 - all started the week with a two-over 74, while major winner Aaron Rai struggled to an opening-round 76.

Chacarra and McIlroy take positives from start

Rory McIlroy, following a three-under 69 : "Anything in the 60s today I felt was a good score. And sort of held it together nicely when I needed to. It was nice to finish with a birdie at the last, and obviously in a pretty good position going into the next few days."

Race to Dubai leader Eugenio Chacarra : " I need to do a couple of things better to be able to have a chance on Sunday, and that's what I'm going to focus on. I think if I fix those, a little strategy-wise and I can putt a little better, I think I'm going to have a chance.

Joost Luiten, following his opening-round 67: "A good opening round. Had a great front nine, five under after nine, then you hope you can push on. The wind picked up and I made two annoying bogeys on 11 and 12. I'm quite happy finishing five under."

articles.title: Chacarra siente el aliento de McIlroy
articles.standfirst: El madrileño no pasa del par, tres golpes peor que el norirlandés, pero Patrick Reed tira un 75, que lo descarta para la Race to Dubai
articles.summary: El madrileño no pasa del par, tres golpes peor que el norirlandés, pero Patrick Reed tira un 75, que lo descarta para la Race to Dubai
articles.body: En la primera meta volante de la etapa final del DP World Tour, Eugenio López-Chacarra ha pasado líder. Por poco pero se mantiene primero. En un jueves de viento, que complicó muchísimo el recorrido dubaití de Jumeirah, el madrileño firmó el par (72) del campo, un resultado que le dejó en vigésimotercera posición ante la creciente amenaza de Rory McIlroy (69), que ya es tercero. La primera noticia positiva es que Patrick Reed que, en esencia, necesita un puesto entre los dos primeros, tiró 75 golpes y está descartado. Por el abultado tanteo y por las prestaciones del estadounidense en esta parte del curso. Chacarra tuvo media hora de genio que le valió para salvar el día. Enlazó tres birdies entre el hoyo 7 y el 9 jugando como el que lo inventó. Tiros largos a calle, golpes a green, putts metibles. Fue, en fin, el momento que enseñó que este jugador no ha llegado donde está por fortuna. Lo acreditan tres victorias y 31 semanas dando el callo. Ganará la Orden de Mérito o no el próximo domingo, pero lo ha peleado como nadie. (Resultados) Esos tres aciertos, otro más en el 5 con un putt desde 10 metros, lo contrarrestaron cuatro bogeys, tres de ellos en pares 3. Especialmente dolió el del seis, un error con el putt que parecía dado. Lo cierto es que le faltó más precisión con los hierros para haber acabado en rojos y más cerca de McIlroy, la estrella con la que compartió partido y que, pese a su 69, no tuvo un buen día en los greenes. El ganador del Masters de Augusta persigue su octava Orden de Mérito con la que igualar a Colin Montgomerie. Se posicionó bien. "Estoy orgulloso de la pelea", apuntó Eugenio. Obviamente, hay muchas cosas que mejorar. Creo que cometí un par de errores estratégicos, pero si logro corregir eso y patear mejor, podré tener una oportunidad el domingo. Sólo necesito poder limpiar un poco la tarjeta de bogeys en los próximos días". Mientras Jon Rahm, que necesita ganar para tener una opción de repetir la victoria final en la clasificación general como en 2019 -sólo él y Seve lo han logrado entre los españoles- no pasó del 71. Estuvo fallón desde el tee -cogió 6 de 14 calles- y la mayoría de los hoyos se convirtieron en un ejercicio de recuperación en un campo que se jugó ligeramente por encima del par (72,52 golpes de media). Su virtuosismo con las manos le permitieron cuatro birdies que enjugaron los tres errores que se dejó por el camino. Peleando por un billete para el PGA Tour la próxima temporada, Jorge Campillo y David Puig dispararon sendos 70. Pero necesitarán mejorar los tres días siguientes para fabricarse una oportunidad. Manda Joost Luiten, el amigo de Johan Cruyff, con 67 golpes.

articles.title: DP World Tour Championship: Rory McIlroy best placed Race to Dubai contender after first round
articles.summary: Rory McIlroy makes a strong start to his bid for a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title with a three under opening round at the DP World Tour Championship.
articles.body:
DP World Tour Championship first-round leaderboard

5 J Luiten (Ned); -4 JS Olesen (Den); -3 V Perez (Fra), G De Leo (Ita), F Schott (Ger), F Laporta (Ita), R McIlroy (NI)

Selected others: -2 T Hatton (Eng); -1 D Hillier (NZ), J Rahm (Spa); E E Chacarra (Spa), M Wallace (Eng); +2 E Ferguson (Sco), R Fox (NZ), C Jarvis (SA), J Schaper (SA); +3 P Reed (US); +4 T Fleetwood (Eng), A Rai (Eng)

Rory McIlroy made a strong start to his bid for a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title with a three-under-par opening round at the DP World Tour Championship.

The world number two, whose round included five birdies and two bogeys in windy conditions, is two shots behind early leader Joost Luiten.

Spain's Eugenio Chacarra, who leads McIlroy by 533.93 points in the Race to Dubai standings - with 2,000 available to this week's winner - opened with a level-par 72, while third-placed American Patrick Reed struggled during a 75.

"I think it was a pretty fair score," said six-time major winner McIlroy.

"I could probably stand here and argue that I could have been better, but I could probably stand here and argue that I could have been worse as well.

"I hit the ball well for the most part. It's tricky, the wind makes it tricky. The course set-up is a little more difficult than in previous years.

"The greens are not like Yas Links (in Abu Dhabi) last week. They're not absolutely perfect, so you've got to have your patience a little bit on them too. Overall, happy with the score."

Nine players - Chacarra, McIlroy, Reed, Casey Jarvis, Aaron Rai, Jon Rahm, Ryan Fox, Jayden Schaper and Daniel Hillier - can still clinch the Race to Dubai, but only Chacarra and McIlroy can guarantee the season-long accolade with victory at Jumeirah Golf Estates this week.

Northern Ireland's McIlroy, who is aiming to match Scotland's Colin Montgomerie's record of eight season-long crowns, birdied two of his opening four holes before giving a shot back at the fifth.

He birdied the seventh and 11th, and while he took six at the par-five 14th, he finished with a two-putt birdie four to end joint third.

"You can't win it on the first day, but you can certainly lose it," added McIlroy.

"I played nicely, so there was never any threat of me shooting a bad one.

"But it was possible today to go out there and shoot a couple over and feel like you were sort of out of the tournament.

"To get off to a solid start was very important."

Chacarra, who has won three times already this season, finished his front nine with three straight birdies to turn in two-under 34 but dropped shots at 13 and 15 to lie five back of Luiten.

Rahm, who catapulted himself into contention last week in Abu Dhabi, by winning his first tournament since leaving LIV Golf, mixed four birdies and three bogeys in an opening 71 to sit alongside New Zealand's Hillier.

Jarvis (+2), Schaper (+2), Fox (+2), Rai (+4) all have work to do, while England's Tommy Fleetwood also struggled in an opening 76.

Dutchman Luiten, the lowest-ranked player in the field, turned in five under but cancelled two birdies with two bogeys on the back nine to settle for a 67, one clear of Denmark's Jacob Skov Olesen.

articles.title: DP World Tour Championship: Rory McIlroy 'trending well' in pursuit of record-equalling Race to Dubai victory
articles.summary: Rory McIlroy chases a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title to match Colin Montgomerie's total; McIlroy has topped the Order of Merit four seasons running but needs to overtake Eugenio Chacarra in the standings at the DP World Tour Championship
articles.body:
McIlroy arrived at the season-ending DP World Tour Championship second in the season-long standings, with the world No 2 looking to win the Race to Dubai for an eighth time and a fifth year in a row .

Winning the Harry Vardon Trophy would see him match Colin Montgomerie's tally of eight Order of Merit titles, with McIlroy making a strong start by posting an opening-round 69 at Jumeirah Golf Estates.

McIlroy moved within two shots of early leader Joost Luiten and three strokes clear of Eugenio Chacarra, the player ahead of him in the rankings, with McGinley expecting the Northern Irishman to keep pushing forward and contend for more Dubai success.

"When he's got a finishing point in mind and a goal that he really wants to achieve, he generally delivers," McGinley told Sky Sports . "This means a lot to him to surpass Monty [Colin Montgomerie].

"I think he's going to be right here until the end. Whether he gets over the line or not, we don't know - golf is not that predictable, but I like where he's at. I think he's trending well and he was the outstanding player of the leading players today [first round].

"We talk about his game evolving, but I think his mind has evolved as well too. It's very hard to go out and put in the 101 per cent effort week in, week out with all the other stuff that he's got going on in his life.

"What you're seeing now is a McIlroy who's picking his battles. Obviously winning majors is a big part of that and he's getting better at that, with two Masters in the last two years, and we're starting to see this Order of Merit become more important to him.

"I don't think we're going to see him maybe back to the world No 1 again, because that takes two years of consistency and that's not where he's at the moment - he's more concerned with other battles that are more important to him.

"He wants to be the outstanding, unquestionable best European player of all time and he's certainly on the way to that. Winning more Order of Merits than everybody else is a big part of that, on top of winning majors."

Nine players entered the week with a mathematical chance of winning the Race to Dubai, but Chacarra, McIlroy and Patrick Reed were the only three who could potentially move to No 1 without winning the season finale.

Reed made an over-par start as Casey Jarvis, Jayden Schaper, Aaron Rai and Ryan Fox - all requiring a victory and results to go their way - also failed to break bar, seeing their slip Race to Dubai hopes fade.

"Some guys have taken themselves out of the equation in terms of the Race to Dubai, but I think this tournament is open," McGinley added. "McIlroy looked particularly good, but Chacarra is not going to roll over easily!

"I think it's three-horse race - Rahm's still a factor and I thought, coming into this week, that McIlroy, Chacarra and Rahm were the three with the best chance.

"Patrick Reed came out of the blocks really early and got a lot of ranking points at the start of the season, but he's gone off form in the last couple of months and it's no surprise to see him drifting away.

"A few guys have come to the party this year that McIlroy might not have had in previous years. It's not as straightforward to win the Race to Dubai as it might have been in previous years - McIlroy knows he's in a battle."

McIlroy claimed his maiden Order of Merit in 2012 before winning back-to-back titles from 2014, with the now 37-year-old proud of his longevity.

"I've never lost my enthusiasm for the game," McIlroy said after his opening round. "This game can beat you down at times and make you quite cynical - I've never let it get to me like that.

"I've seen some others throughout the years, where it has gotten to them a little bit. I've always tried to be grateful that I get to play this game for a living.

"I think that gratitude and that enthusiasm to go to the golf course and compete every day, I've never lost that. Hopefully I never will lose that until I decide to hang 'em up."

articles.title: Kai Trump's Status for The Annika Golf Tournament Confirmed After Surgery on Wrist Injury
articles.summary: Miami golfer Kai Trump, the granddaughter of U.S. President Donald Trump, will officially miss her second shot at LPGA action after undergoing wrist surgery.
articles.body:
Miami golfer Kai Trump, the granddaughter of U.S. President Donald Trump, will officially miss her second shot at LPGA action after undergoing wrist surgery .

Hurricanes golfer Scarlett Schremmer told to Golfweek's Beth Ann Nichols she will be playing this week while Trump will sit out The Annika at Pelican Golf Club.

Miami had announced Oct. 15 Schremmer had received a sponsor invitation to The Annika. Trump had made her LPGA debut on sponsor invitation at the event last November.

Schremmer is expecting Trump to be present at the Florida golf course for Thursday's opening round, Nichols reported.

Trump announced in an Oct. 14 social media post she had undergone surgery on a wrist injury suffered during her first tournament of the collegiate season, the Golfweek Fall Classic at Pawleys Island in South Carolina.

She previously said she "felt like she tore" something in her wrist during the September tournament.

This marked the second wrist surgery Trump has undergone within the past year. She previously announced the completion of a procedure on her left wrist last January.

In Trump's first appearance at The Annika, she went 18-over through two rounds to finish last in the 108-player field and miss the cut.

She has appeared in two collegiate tournaments prior to undergoing surgery, starting when she finished 102nd out of 120 competitors at Pawleys Island.

Trump most recently placed 13th in a 14-player field in October at the Golfweek Put Me In Coach Invitational in Muncie, Indiana.

articles.title: Dan Hicks, longtime NBC sportscaster, dies at 64
articles.summary: Hicks got his start on TV with CNN in 1989 before joining NBC Sports, where he had worked since 1992.
articles.body:
Longtime sportscaster Dan Hicks has died at the age of 64, it was announced by his wife, Hannah Storm .

According to the family, Hicks had been dealing with an "acute illness."

"Our family is heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected passing of Dan following an acute illness," Storm said in a statement. "He was a devoted husband of over 30 years, loving father to our three daughters, and cherished friend to so many. His loss is immeasurable. "Dan was truly one of a kind and, quite simply, the person everyone wanted to be around. When he walked into a room, he brought the energy, the laughter and the people together. He was endlessly kind, thoughtful and funny, and he made everyone feel like they mattered. "Our three daughters and I are heartbroken. We are grateful for the love and support surrounding our family during this incredibly difficult time. There are simply no words to express how much he will be missed."

"Dan Hicks was an extraordinary colleague, friend and person," NBC Sports' Rick Cordella, Sam Flood and Molly Solomon said in a statement. articles.title: Sports world reacts to the sudden passing of legendary broadcaster Dan Hicks at the age of 64
articles.summary: Hannah Storm shared news of Dan Hicks' sudden passing from an acute illness, calling the NBC golf and Olympics voice a devoted husband and father.
articles.body: Dan Hicks, the longtime sportscaster best known for his work covering golf and the Olympics, has passed away at the age of 64. Hicks had been the lead announcer for NBC's golf coverage since 2000 and the stroke-by-stroke announcer for Olympic swimming since the 1996 Games held in Atlanta, Georgia, and was responsible for one of the most memorable calls in Olympic history while on the mic for Team USA's comeback victory in the men's 4x100 freestyle involving Michael Phelps during the 2008 Games. Hannah Storm, Hicks' wife and well-known ESPN anchor, shared the tragic news about Hicks' passing on Thursday morning. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "Our family is heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected passing of Dan following an acute illness," Storm's statement began. "He was a devoted husband of over 30 years, loving father to our three daughters, and cherished friend to so many. His loss is immeasurable. "Dan was truly one of a kind and, quite simply, the person everyone wanted to be around. When he walked into a room, he brought the energy, the laughter and the people together. He was endlessly kind, thoughtful and funny, and he made everyone feel like they mattered. "Our three daughters and I are heartbroken. We are grateful for the love and support surrounding our family during this incredibly difficult time. There are simply no words to express how much he will be missed." SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER With Hicks being the lead voice of NBC and Golf Channel's coverage for the last 26 years, he is, in many respects, the voice of the sport for an entire generation of fans. Among his countless memorable moments in the golf broadcasting booth came during the 2008 U.S. Open at Torrey Pines, when Tiger Woods made a birdie putt on the 72nd hole to force a playoff against Rocco Mediate. Hicks letting the monumental moment breathe before hitting fans with the question of "Expect anything different?" will live on forever. Hicks, a University of Arizona graduate, began his broadcasting career in radio before becoming a sports reporter for CNN in 1989 and eventually moving to NBC Sports in 1992. articles.title: Club Champion Launches New Site To Fix Custom Fitting Misconceptions
articles.summary: Club Champion unveiled a redesigned website on November 10, 2026, aiming to clarify that custom fitting requires precise building, not just a swing test.
articles.body:
Club Champion, the world's leading custom golf club fitter, rolled out a newly redesigned website on November 10, 2026, to clarify a persistent confusion among golfers. The digital overhaul focuses on education, showing players that a fitting session is only half the equation for better performance. Many golfers assume that any club fitting leads to identical results, regardless of who performs it or how the clubs are built afterward. This new platform aims to correct that view by highlighting the necessity of precision custom club building alongside the fitting process itself.

The company's goal is to demonstrate that identifying the right equipment is merely the starting point. A true fitting determines the exact combination of clubhead, shaft, length, loft, lie, and swingweight needed to optimize a player's game. However, those results vanish if the delivered clubs do not match the specifications found during the session. Club Champion differentiates itself by combining Tour-level fitting technology with brand-agnostic equipment selection and expert Master Fitters. Club Champion's approach ensures the final product matches the data captured in the fitting bay.

According to Plugged In Golf , the new website addresses the misconception that all club fittings are created equal. Nick Sherburne, the Founder and Chief Operating Officer of Club Champion, directly explained the issue. "I think one of the biggest misconceptions in golf is that a fitting is a fitting," said Sherburne. He noted that without precision custom club building, the value of an advanced fitting is significantly reduced. From the initial swing within the fitting bay through to the final club received in hand, the company offers a full solution for golfers.

According to Plugged In Golf, the updated website enables golfers across all skill levels to grasp the necessity of an exact-specification build. The goal is to remove intimidation rather than create it. "We fit golfers of all abilities, but we also understand that not everyone comes to us with the same level of knowledge," said Sherburne.

The conversation around equipment performance often centers on forgiveness, a metric deeply tied to moment of inertia (MOI). Golf Digest reported on March 8, 2026, that equipment rulemakers were concerned about the extent of forgiveness available twenty years ago. The USGA issued a notice setting a limit on MOI because they feared "the extent to which a good result can be achieved from a less than ideal contact with the ball." The regulator worried that further increases to MOI could reduce the challenge of the game by lowering the skill required to hit the ball straight.

Despite those limits set in 2005, Golf Digest noted that drivers are more forgiving than ever before. Manufacturers have found ways to make clubs easier to use while staying within the legal MOI limit of 6,000 grams-centimeters. Ryan Stokke, Ping's director of product design, emphasized the balance required in modern driver construction. "You need to have high MOI, but it needs to be coupled with a proper center of gravity (CG) location for a certain player," he said. This combination allows for adjustability that matches a player's specific swing tendencies.

K Wayne Johnson, a 7-handicap golfer tested in the Golf Digest Hot List 2026, described the feeling of using a highly forgiving driver like the Ping G440. "You feel like you can't miss with this one. Just point it out towards the fairway and swing. It just doesn't seem to veer right or left at all. It gets up quickly and goes far." Johnson's experience highlights why forgiveness remains a top priority for players seeking to improve their scores. The new Club Champion website aims to help golfers find these specific combinations of forgiveness and custom fit.

articles.title: Patrick Reed Targets Top Ten And Ryder Cup Spot For 2027
articles.summary: Patrick Reed returns to the PGA Tour with clear goals. He wants to win again, hit the top ten, and wear red, white, and blue in 2027.
articles.body:
Patrick Reed is back on the PGA Tour and he has zero interest in playing it safe. The 2018 Masters champion just secured his card for 2027, but his real focus is on reclaiming his spot among the elite. He wants to win tournaments and climb back into the world top ten. This isn't a retirement tour; it is a full-court press to prove he still belongs at the top of the game.

Reed made his intentions clear during a press conference in Dubai on November 10. Although the path returning from LIV Golf is difficult, he has already secured two wins on the DP World Tour this season. By winning the Hero Dubai Desert Classic and Qatar Masters, he secured his position within the top 10 of the Race to Dubai standings. He is now set to play at the Austin Championship, where the field of 120 players will battle for a $6 million purse. The winner takes home $1.08 million and 500 FedExCup points. Reed is not just looking to participate; he wants to dominate.

Reed understands that finishing high in the rankings is not enough if the trophy case stays empty. He feels that restoring his ability to win tournaments and boosting his world ranking will be key elements in his plans for next season. He laid out his roadmap in no uncertain terms during his recent interview. "Go out and get back to the winners' circle on the PGA Tour like I was right before I left… Go out there and assert myself into the top ten in the world again," Reed said, according to Yahoo Sports . That is a bold statement for a player who left the tour in 2022, but he has the wins on the DP World Tour to back up the confidence.

While Reed secures his future, many of his former LIV Golf colleagues face an uncertain road. The PGA Tour is delaying decisions on return pathways until LIV's bankruptcy proceedings conclude, which could stretch into 2027. Reed, however, avoided the worst of that uncertainty by leaving LIV earlier this year. Despite his own success, he refused to gloat about the struggles of those who stayed behind. Reed said, "I don't really get any satisfaction," speaking about observing. other players encounter suspensions and uncertainty. He added that "You never want to see guys struggle or have to sit out," showing a side of the player that goes beyond the usual competitive fire.

The biggest prize on Reed's horizon is not a paycheck; it is the chance to wear the red, white, and blue again. Since 2018 he has not competed in a Ryder Cup, yet he is eager to rejoin the team at Adare Manor in Ireland. "It would mean everything. Any time I can represent United States and wear red, white and blue means a lot for me," he said. When asked specifically about returning to the American team, he didn't hesitate. "Oh, it would mean everything," he said. The Austin Championship starts on November 9, and Reed has his sights set on a long-term victory.

articles.body: Dustin Johnson has created an impressive financial portfolio from big wins on the golf course, big payouts from tournaments and his move to LIV Golf. He has mixed elite sporting accomplishment with business ventures and a lifestyle connected to some of the wealthiest personalities in golf.His private life has also been in the spotlight. Johnson married model and media personality Paulina Gretzky in April 2022, uniting two families with notable sporting pedigrees. The couple’s life in Florida, their luxury properties and taste for high-end leisure activities have fuelled public interest in their world of wealth, as has Gretzky, daughter of NHL legend Wayne Gretzky.How Dustin Johnson and Paulina Gretzky built their estimated $105 million fortuneThe couple’s alleged wealth is primarily due to Dustin Johnson’s golf earnings. Johnson’s PGA Tour and major championship earnings total about $97 million, while his LIV Golf earnings are about $54.1 million, according to figures compiled by Front Office Sports as of May 2025. The publication estimated his lifetime earnings at about $166.6 million at that time. These are reported career earnings, not his current net worth.His earnings structure took a big jump in 2022 when he switched to LIV Golf. The deal brought considerable financial attention to his career and put him among the big names linked to LIV Golf's expansion.Johnson was also named captain of 4Aces GC. His official LIV Golf profile lists him as the team’s captain and highlights his individual wins, including the first-ever 2022 LIV Golf Individual Championship.The impact of tournament performances and team success on Johnson’s earnings has persisted beyond the original contract. Born into a high-profile sporting family and always in the public eye, it was her modelling and entertainment work that built her own profile.The pair tied the knot in April of 2022 at Tennessee’s Blackberry Farm after several years together. They have two sons, Tatum and River. Gretzky has been spotted with Johnson at golf tournaments and public events on many occasions, and their family life continues to be a hot topic of interest for sports and entertainment followers.Their lifestyle also suggests a liking for luxury travel, waterfront living and high-end leisure. articles.title: The Annika: Nelly Korda makes impressive return to LPGA Tour action to trail Minami Katsu and Hye-Jin Choi by two shots
articles.summary: Nelly Korda sits two shots off lead after opening round on return to action; Minami Katsu and Korean Hye-Jin share lead; Lottie Woad and Leona Maguire four shots back; Watch round two of The Annika on LPGA Tour from 4pm on Friday, live on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
Korda, whose last competitive golf came at the Solheim Cup in September after her most recent LPGA Tour outing in August, shot a bogey-free seven-under par round of 63 at Pelican Golf Club in Florida.

Korda trails Japan's Minami Katsu and Korean Hye-Jin Choi by two shots, with fellow American Lindy Duncan also ahead of her on eight under after making a hole-in-one during her 62.

"It was nice to kind of feel those juices flowing again, especially playing with Hye-Jin who just had a great round today," Korda said.

She already has clinched LPGA player of the year based on points, and Korda can qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame with a victory in one of the final two events of the season.

Denmark's Nicole Broch Estrup and Spain's Julia Lopez Ramirez are the top two Europeans as they sit in a group of four players tied for fifth on six under.

England's Lottie Woad and Ireland's Leona Maguire are part of a group of 11 players tied for ninth on five under, which also includes Spain's Carlota Ciganda.

Charley Hull, who sits eighth, a place behind compatriot Woad in the world rankings, finished a shot further back on four under.

Allisen Corpuz joined Duncan in carding a hole-in-one at the par-three third hole, but was only able to post three-under par.

Co-leader Choi, coming off a strong Asia swing that included a pair of runner-up finishes, is looking for her first LPGA title in five years as a member. Her game travelled well from Asia to the Gulf Coast of Florida, with birdies on half her holes for 63.

Katsu played in the afternoon and ran off three straight birdies late in her round to catch Choi at 61.

Choi said she can struggle with the Florida grass, especially around the greens. That wasn't a problem on Thursday when she hit 17 greens in regulation.

Katsu also played bogey-free as she tries to become the sixth Japanese player to win on the LPGA Tour this year.

So much attention was on Korda, who captured two majors early in the season. Her last tournament was the FM Championship outside Boston and then the Solheim Cup, where Korda went 2-1-1 in an American loss in the Netherlands.

"I needed to take that break, and right after Solheim I was burned out," Korda said. "I just needed to mentally step away for a few days."

She typically skips the Asia swing, early and late in the year, and then gears up for the final two LPGA events in Florida.

Korda has four wins this year, but not since the big one - her first US Women's Open title in early June at Riviera. She leads the Race to CME Globe, although next week at the Tour Championship any of the 60 players in the field can become the season champion who gets a $2m prize.

Also at stake for Korda this week is a chance to surpass Annika Sorenstam, the tournament host, on the career money list.

"What drives me is the competitive tournament that I'm in currently," Korda said. "I want to do the best that I possibly can where I currently am."

articles.title: She spends five months alone in the Wyoming mountains watching over 600 cattle: Meet Brittany Heseltine, the woman doing one of America's toughest ranching jobs
articles.summary: Imagine spending five months in the wilderness, far away from the conveniences of modern life, with no bustling neighbourhood, no regular office hours,
articles.body: Imagine spending five months in the wilderness, far away from the conveniences of modern life, with no bustling neighbourhood, no regular office hours, and barely anyone around to have a chat with. Your closest companions are a few horses, working dogs and hundreds of cattle spread across vast mountain pastures. Your mornings begin at dawn, your days are spent riding across rugged terrain, and your responsibilities… well, they include keeping an eye out for predators, treating sick animals, and ensuring that an entire herd stays safe.For most people, this might sound like an extreme survival challenge. But not for Brittany Heseltine; for her, it’s her way of life.If you picture five months alone in the Wyoming mountains, with no city lights, no grocery stores, not even a neighbor peering over the fence, you start to get a sense of Brittany Heseltine’s world.Her company? A couple of trusty horses, four hard-working dogs, and as many as 800 cattle grazing wherever the grass takes them. There aren’t really any days off or lazy mornings here. Heseltine wakes at dawn, moves through wild country on horseback, and spends the rest of the day corralling straggling calves, doctoring the sick, and keeping a wary eye out for grizzly bears and wolves. Some people might call it isolation. For her, it’s freedom.Who is Brittany Heseltine?Brittany Heseltine, a working cowgirl and range rider in Wyoming, United States, Heseltine has one of the more unusual and demanding jobs in American ranching. She isn’t just punching a clock. As a range rider and foreman for the Upper Green River Cattle Association, she is the living, breathing version of someone who found her calling and ran with it. It’s a life built on self-reliance. Each summer, as soon as the grass greens up, she loads up her horses and heads deep into the Bridger-Teton National Forest. There, amid mountain peaks and rivers tucked into the folds of the land, Heseltine and a small crew watch over hundreds of cattle, spread out across miles of wilderness.Heseltine first made waves outside her community when CBS’s 60 Minutes ran a story on her. The images alone were striking: Heseltine guiding a string of cows through a mountain pass, her face sunburned from days in the open, barely a hint of the outside world. In that first feature, she looked after about 600 cattle. By 2025, with more experience under her belt, she was a foreman overseeing 800 head and taking responsibility not just for the herd, but for a handful of other range riders as well.Five months in the wilderness: What does Brittany Heseltine’s daily routine look like?Heseltine’s routine is more demanding than most of us can really grasp. Most days start with a cup of coffee as the sun slips over the mountains. Then she’ll saddle up, check gear, and ride out with her dogs to find the herds. She can pick up on the subtlest change, like the flick of an ear, a shift in the way cattle graze. Someone else might miss it, but Heseltine knows this means something’s off. Maybe a cow’s showing signs of illness. Maybe a predator’s nearby. She doesn’t just ride for miles; she pays relentless attention, reading not just the animals but the land itself, figuring out where the grass is thickest, when it’s time to move the herd to fresh ground, all without a blueprint or feature film soundtrack.Grizzly bears, wolves and the dangers of working aloneThe biggest threats usually have teeth. Grizzly bears are part of the scenery here, cracks in the brush that turn out not to be wind but a shifting shadow. Wolves run these valleys, too: brilliant, quick, unafraid of cattle when the pack’s hungry. Heseltine doesn’t pretend she’s fearless. She counts bears she’s seen, and more she’s only sensed. She’s learned to be fast with a rope and steady with a dart gun. If a calf limps away from the herd, she won’t hesitate. She ropes it, checks for wounds or sickness, and administers whatever care it needs — all of this without backup, miles from the nearest vet.On top of wrangling livestock and dodging predators, she has to be a one-woman vet clinic. Whenever something goes wrong, be it foot rot, pneumonia, or pink eye, Heseltine isn’t paging anyone for help. She carries the medicine, the syringes. It’s all on her. When larger animals need attention, she uses specialised techniques and equipment, including a dart gun.What is the Green River Drift? The historic cattle trail behind her jobNow, working alone in the wilderness brings challenges most of us can only imagine. Summer storms blow in fast, turning dirt roads into rivers of mud. A misstep by horse or rider can mean a broken bone, hours or days from help. Her trailer or cabin rarely has running water, and cell service is more a rumor than a reality. For months, her world becomes this wild sweep of pasture and predators, punctuated by the simple rhythm of sunup and sundown.But the history behind her work gives it a sense of grounding and meaning. The Green River Drift, a cattle trail that’s been used since the 1890s, is woven into Wyoming’s identity. Every spring, ranchers push thousands of cattle up this route from valley ranches to higher mountain pastures. Once the cows are settled, it’s up to the range riders, Heseltine being among them, to keep them safe all summer. In autumn, as temperatures drop, the cattle make their way back down, retracing the trail, and closing another chapter in ranching history. The Drift is so important, in fact, that it’s now protected as a Traditional Cultural Property and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2014 — the first ranching location in the country to receive that designation.What keeps Brittany Heseltine coming back?Heseltine has said it herself: it just fits. She loves the quiet mornings when mist rises off the meadows, the satisfaction of helping a sick calf stand again, even the grit it takes to survive months cut off from everyday life. Sure, it gets lonely, especially in the middle of a summer storm or when night sets in so deep you can’t see your own hand. But she keeps returning, year after year, because it’s more than a hard job to her; it’s a way of staying connected to something wild and elemental.Heseltine’s life is a throwback to an older kind of America, one that doesn’t get much attention. But now, people have started to take notice of her story beyond the ranching community. She’s been a guest on podcasts, featured by agricultural groups, and earned praise from people who see her as a trailblazer for women in a field still largely dominated by men. But praise isn’t why she rides. She does it for the land, the animals, and that feeling of freedom only the mountains can offer.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
