articles.title: DP World Tour Championship: Rory McIlroy takes share of lead alongside Tyrrell Hatton in Race to Dubai finale
articles.summary: Rory McIlroy surged to take a share of the lead at the DP World Tour Championship, joining Tyrrell Hatton at the top of the leaderboard at five under par; watch the third round of the DP World Tour Championship live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
McIlroy briefly held the outright lead on Friday after he went four-under through his first 11 holes, but a flurry of bogeys on his back nine saw the Northern Irishman drop down the leaderboard at the Jumeirah Golf Estates.

He then hit back with a birdie on the 18th, which saw the two-time Masters champion post a second-round 70 and move to join clubhouse leader Hatton at five under par.

Hatton began his round in emphatic fashion, making birdies on his first two holes, before mixing in a further three birdies alongside two bogeys to post a three-under 69 for his second round. He will tee up with McIlroy in Saturday's final pairing .

Overnight leader, Joost Luiten, also suffered a late stumble, conceding back-to-back bogeys on holes 14 and 15, but unlike McIlroy, he was unable to recover, going one over for the day to join Kristoffer Reitan tied for third at four under par.

McIlroy's hopes of equalling Collin Montgomerie's record of eight Order of Merit titles grew, as Race to Dubai Rankings leader Eugenio Chacarra battled to stay within touching distance of the leaders, mixing in six birdies with five bogeys to go one over through 16 holes.

However, the Spaniard showed resilience, carding back-to-back birdies on his final two holes, even chipping in from off the green on the 18th, to post a second-round 71, and move four shots off the leaders.

Patrick Reed, who had been vying to become only the second American to win the Race to Dubai title, endured a torrid day, posting a five-over 77, and slumped to second-bottom on the leaderboard after going six over in his final six holes.

McIlroy's performance, meanwhile, moves him to the top of the projected Race to Dubai rankings.

"I want to win the tournament," McIlroy said. "And if I win the tournament, that's all I can do. It doesn't really matter what any of the other guys do, if they play well enough.

"But if I go and I win the first trophy on Sunday, then the second trophy should take care of itself."

Late bogeys were the order of the day at the Earth Course, with Mikael Lindberg, who had also briefly moved to take a share of the lead on Friday, dropping two shots late on as he fell off the pace to join Freddy Schott and Victor Perez at three under par.

Jon Rahm battled with bunkers throughout his second round, first taking two out of a fairway bunker on the seventh hole on his way to making a par, before smashing a wedge shot into the bank of another bunker on the eighth hole, as he posted a second-round 71 to finish three shots back from Hatton and McIlroy.

"I was making good swings, I just couldn't quite hit it close enough to have makeable putts," Rahm said.

"I hit loads of greens, I was just never constantly over 30 feet. It's going to be hard to make putts like that. So it's a bit of a survival day."

It took McIlroy a while to find his rhythm, with the Northern Irishman missing early birdie chances on holes one and two before opening his account on the third, flighting a wedge shot at the flag to set him up for a short birdie putt.

He added back-to-back birdies on the seventh and eighth, with McIlroy showcasing his exceptional iron play to hit the green on the former from 240 yards out.

His back nine was a different story, despite McIlroy again showcasing his elite accuracy to make a birdie on the 10th.

McIlroy came unstuck on the 12th, sending his tee shot left, before missing the green with his approach as he went on to card his first bogey of the day.

"Once you start putting yourself out of position on this golf course, this setup, these conditions, it starts to get very difficult," McIlroy said.

He then came a cropper to a fairway bunker on hole 16 and missed the green on the par-three 17th to make back-to-back bogeys late on.

But he responded with a birdie on the final hole, sending an approach from 267 yards out to the heart of the green to leave himself a 72ft eagle putt.

He couldn't make good his first attempt, with McIlroy ultimately wrapping up his second round with a birdie.

articles.summary: El norirlandés, que fue líder en solitario, firma dos bogeys en los segundos nueve hoyos y el español sólo está a cuatro golpes de su principal rival por la general europea
articles.body: Rory McIlroy tiene un emirato en Dubái, el terreno donde ha levantado siete títulos en su carrera, cuatro en el Dessert Classic, tres en la final del DP World Tour, el torneo que acontece esta semana y en la que el viernes, complicado por el viento y con unos greenes secos y duros, alcanzó el liderato compartido con Tyrrell Hatton. Es la plaza en la que no necesita echar más cuentas para ganar por octava vez la Orden de Mérito e igualar a la leyenda Colin Montgomerie, el mejor golfista de la historia sin grandes. En el ecuador de la pelea por la ahora bautizada Race to Dubái se ha quedado prácticamente en un pulso entre el norirlandés y Eugenio López-Chacarra, que ha cedido el liderato provisional. Pese a ello, el español que ha ganado tres torneos esta temporada, salió del Jumeirah Golf Estates lanzando el puño y con un "vamos, vamos". Acababa de embocar un chip para birdie en el hoyo 18 y firmar un 71, uno bajo par, en un día 'perete': 5, 6 y 7. Cinco bogeys, seis birdies y siete pares. (Resultados) "He cometido muchos errores, a pesar de que también he logrado muchos birdies, y eso me ha impedido encontrar ese momento para impulsarme", expuso Chacarra, que cogió apenas ocho calles. "De todos modos, en esas malas condiciones también he tenido muchos aciertos y eso me anima para los 36 hoyos que quedan. SI Rory, que juega siempre bien en este campo, gana, pues se llevará la Race to Dubái y ya está. Pero yo también voy a pelear por la victoria. Así que vamos a ver". Lo cierto es que todo queda en el aire. Apenas son cuatro golpes entre ambos. El undécimo puesto provisional de Eugenio le valdría si Rory no acaba entre los dos primeros en solitario. "Está el campo muy difícil", advierte el doble ganador del Masters de Augusta que lo bordó al comienzo, con cuatro birdies en 10 hoyos, pero luego llegaron los problemas. No pegó el driver con la facilidad que lo había hecho y cosechó tres bogeys. El acierto final en el 18 le otorgó un valioso 70. A Chacarra le ayudará que muchos se agolpen el domingo para la victoria y alguno puede arrebatarle el triunfo a McIlroy, lo que potenciaría sus opciones. Entre ellos está colocado Jon Rahm, octavo a tres golpes como David Puig. Sin la magia de la semana pasada, dejó dos birdies, en sendos pares 5, y un bogey, para otro 71. Falló menos calles que el jueves, pero luego no las dejó cerca. "Si no estás en la calle, prácticamente no tienes ninguna posibilidad de hacer un birdie y tienes que luchar por un cuatro", contó el de Barrika, que no se descarta para la victoria. "Estoy haciendo buenos swings, así que todo puede pasar", avisa. Más sólido esta semana parece Tyrrell Hatton, que va a por su sexto Rolex Series. Y es de los que no se achanta ante nada.

articles.title: DP World Tour Championship: Rory McIlroy and Tyrrell Hatton tied with Race to Dubai leader Eugenio Chacarra four back
articles.summary: Rory McIlroy is tied for the lead at the halfway mark of the season-ending DP World Tour Championship as he chases a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title.
articles.body:
DP World Tour Championship second-round leaderboard

5 T Hatton (Eng), R McIlroy (NI); -4 K Reitan (Nor), J Luiten (Ned); -3 M Lindberg (Swe), F Schott (Ger), V Perez (Fra); -2 J Schaper (SA), J Rahm (Spa), D Puig (Spa)

Selected others: -1 E Chacarra (Spa); E A Scott (Aus), C Hill (Sco); +3 T Fleetwood (Eng); +6 A Rai (Eng); +8 P Reed (US)

Rory McIlroy is tied for the lead at the halfway mark of the season-ending DP World Tour Championship as he chases a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title.

The six-time major winner followed a three-under opening 69 with an up-and-down 70 to join England's Tyrrell Hatton at the top at Jumeirah Golf Estates in Dubai.

Hatton mixed five birdies and two bogeys to shoot 69, while overnight leader Joost Luiten carded a 73 to lie one shot back alongside Norway's Kristoffer Reitan.

McIlroy, who is guaranteed to equal Colin Montgomerie's record haul of eight season-long crowns with victory this week, sits four shots ahead of Race to Dubai leader Eugenio Chacarra.

The Spaniard, who won three times earlier this season to lead the standings entering this week, birdied his final two holes to finish one under.

"I think it's been a bit eye-opening to see the scoring the first two days," said world number two McIlroy.

"I don't think the wind is supposed to be as up over the weekend, so the scoring might be a little bit better.

"As I said, the scoring this week, because of this course set-up, just isn't as good as in previous years. I've been coming back to the golf course for 15 plus years, and you just associate this course with pretty low scoring.

"And then when it's not, you just have to reframe what is a good score. Anything in the 60s, it seems, this week is a good score."

Hunting a fourth DP World Tour Championship win and fifth successive Race to Dubai triumph, McIlroy seized the lead with four birdies in his opening 10 holes.

However, the back-to-back Masters champion's momentum stalled with a bogey five at the 12th and he squandered further shots at the 16th and 17th.

But the world number two made a closing birdie for the second day in a row to secure his place in Saturday's final pairing alongside Ryder Cup team-mate Hatton (08:40 GMT).

While Hatton cannot win the Race to Dubai, he boosted his chances of securing a ninth DP World Tour victory - and first since leaving LIV Golf - with another solid display in windy conditions.

The world number 23 made three birdies in a bogey-free front nine before slipping up at the 10th.

He knocked his approach to two feet to set up another birdie at 15, and while he stumbled at the par-three 17th after finding the greenside bunker, he bounced back with a closing birdie.

"It's been tricky. I thought the back nine played really difficult yesterday," said Hatton, who finished second behind Jon Rahm in Abu Dhabi last week.

"The wind was sort of moving round just enough that it goes from slightly off the right to then more down and club selection just becomes really difficult.

"Today it felt a little bit easier, but then just towards the end there, the wind sort of got stronger than where it was yesterday, so then that makes it more challenging.

"But overall, it's been a solid start to the tournament."

South Africa's Jayden Schaper (68) and Spain's two-time major winner Rahm (71) - both of whom can still clinch the Race to Dubai - are well placed at two under.

However, Patrick Reed's hopes of becoming the second American to lift the Harry Vardon Trophy suffered a significant blow after the 2018 Masters champion followed an opening 75 with a 77.

articles.title: Rory McIlroy boosts Race to Dubai hopes at DP World Tour Championship as Eugenio Chacarra targets weekend fightback
articles.summary: Rory McIlroy heads into the weekend projected to move above Eugenio Chacarra in the Race to Dubai standings; McIlroy shares the halfway lead at the DP World Tour Championship, with Chacarra four back; watch live on Saturday from 7am on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
McIlroy, starting the week behind Chacarra in the standings, needs to finish inside the top four to have any chance of winning the Harry Vardon Trophy for a fifth successive season and match Colin Montgomerie's tally of Order of Merit titles.

The world No 2 posted a second-round 70 at Jumeirah Golf Estates to share the halfway lead on five under with England's Tyrrell Hatton, leaving McIlroy firm favourite to win the season-ending event for a fourth time.

McIlroy currently sits top of the projected Race to Dubai standings and his fast start is no surprise to Chacarra, who delivered a birdie-birdie finish to sit four strokes back and remain in contention for his fourth victory of the season.

"It's just what it is - I knew it [McIlroy impressing] was going to happen," Chacarra admitted after a one-under 71. "It's one of the favourite courses of Rory and he's had so much success here.

"He is obviously one of the best players in the world, so we know it's going to be tough.

"I still have two days. I'm happy with that finish I needed [to second round]. I like how I'm hitting it - there's been a lot of birdies in harder conditions. If I can clean up the card a little, I like my chance on the weekend.

" I can control what I can control. If Rory comes here and wins the tournament, he's a deserved champion - there's nothing I can really do. I'm going to try to win the tournament."

McIlroy becomes favourite for Race to Dubai history

Nine players entered with a mathematical chance of still winning the Race to Dubai title but Jon Rahm and Jayden Schaper - outside of McIlroy and Chacarra - are the only others not over-par at the halfway stage.

"I'm making really good swings," said Rahm. "I'm playing really good golf."

The Spaniard needs to win the tournament, have McIlroy finish outside the top two and see Chacarra place worse than eighth to claim the Race to Dubai title.

"All we can do is keep putting good swings in and I feel like I've done that and hit a lot of good putts. Hopefully I start hitting them [approaches] a little closer on the weekend."

McIlroy stepped onto the 12th tee with a two-shot lead after four early birdies on Friday afternoon, only to bogey three of his next six holes before moving alongside Hatton by taking advantage of the par-five last.

"I played very solidly for those first 11 holes and then the 12th felt like the first time I'd really put myself out of position," McIlroy said. "Once you put yourself out of position on this golf course, this setup, these conditions, it starts to get very, very difficult.

"If you miss a fairway, or even if you miss a green, the lies around the greens aren't very good - it's very, very tricky once you get yourself out of position. Easy to make bogeys, but it was nice to at least birdie the last and feel like I salvaged the day a little bit.

"If anything, I started to get frustrated with the golf course. As it dries out, lies and fairways aren't very good and greens start to get bumpy. I started to get maybe a little bit frustrated with the course on the way in, but I think it's just the nature of it.

"I've won four times down the road at Emirates [Golf Club, Dubai Desert Classic] and it would be nice to win four times here, so I want to win the tournament.

"If I win the tournament, that's all I can do. It doesn't really matter what any of the other guys do, or if they play well enough. If I go and I win the first trophy on Sunday, then the second trophy should take care of itself."

articles.title: Wyndham Clark admits what he really thinks of Jackson Koivun after watching him play at the Presidents Cup
articles.summary: Wyndham Clark got to witness what Jackson Koivun is really like as a golfer and a person at the Presidents Cup back in September at Medinah. The United State...
articles.body:
Wyndham Clark got to witness what Jackson Koivun is really like as a golfer and a person at the Presidents Cup back in September at Medinah.

The United States won the Presidents Cup in the end, but the 17-13 scoreline was a lot closer than many predicted prior to the event.

Clark struggled for his best form throughout the week at Medinah, but Koivun was one of the stars for Team USA.

Jackson Koivun went unbeaten throughout the week at the Presidents Cup , winning two and halving one of his three matches.

Wyndham Clark got a first-hand view that week of how the 21-year-old goes about his business both on and off the golf course.

And now the two-time US Open winner has opened up on his true feelings about the talented young American.

What Wyndham Clark thinks of Jackson Koivun after watching him at the Presidents Cup

Koivun is keen to play on the US Ryder Cup team in 2027, and his performance at the Presidents Cup surely means that he is almost guaranteed to be at Adare Manor next year.

The 21-year-old obviously has the talent and mentality required to succeed at the very highest level of the game, but what does someone who has already reached that level think about the youngster's chances of doing exactly that?

During an appearance on the Dan on Golf YouTube channel, Clark was asked about Koivun as a player and a person and whether he acts older than his tender years.

" I tell you what, I have nothing but praise for that kid. He's so talented. Obviously, he showed it off at the Presidents Cup.

" You know, a lot of people asked a lot of us what we thought of his pick and I said it somewhere, I was like, 'He's our secret weapon'. Because I think, you know, he's a young kid that has nothing to lose. No pressure, really.

" And then, going up against him as, you know, a seasoned veteran, someone like Si Woo Kim. There is more pressure on Si Woo.

" You don't want to lose to the kid, right? And sure enough, that's what happens. So, yeah, nothing but respect for him.

" He is a kid, but I love the kid. He's awesome. He's gonna have a lot of success out here. "

That is a seriously glowing reference of Jackson Koivun, and he will surely be very proud indeed when he hears those remarks from Wyndham Clark.

It will be fascinating to watch how Koivun performs on the PGA Tour in 2027 with his attempts to make the Ryder Cup team at Adare Manor making for a seriously interesting subplot.

articles.title: Patriots Week 10 official game statuses: Good news, bad news

articles.body:
The New England Patriots have already ruled out three players for Sunday's game against the Detroit Lions . However, on Friday, they officially listed nine more players as questionable for the Week 10 matchup.

Running back TreVeyon Henderson, cornerback Carlton Davis III and offensive lineman Ben Brown didn't make the trip and won't be available. Davis being out and backup cornerback Charles Woods being questionable is bad news for the Patriots .

Surprisingly, however, wide receiver A.J. Brown and running back Rhamondre Stevenson are both questionable to play. So there's potential good news for New England.

Brown has been a limited participant at practice throughout the week, and the fact that he hopped on the flight to Germany with a chronic knee issue has led many to believe that he's going to try and play. Patriots coach Mike Vrabel did make it clear that the fact that players made the trip doesn't guarantee they'll be on the field for the game. So we'll have to wait and see with Brown.

The same is the case for Stevenson, who was expected to miss some time with the knee injury that he suffered in last week's game against the Green Bay Packers. articles.title: More Americans are playing golf than ever before. Here's why
articles.summary: Golf participation has reached a record high of 49.5 million Americans, driven by simulators and new venues.
articles.body:
Golf has officially reached a new high-water mark.

And this time, Tiger Woods isn't the only reason. More Americans are playing golf than at any point in history. But the game's latest surge isn't just happening on the golf course. It's happening in garages, sports bars, indoor simulators and entertainment venues across the country.

An estimated 30.8 million Americans played golf on a traditional golf course in 2026, according to research from the National Golf Foundation (NGF). That's an increase of 1.7 million players over the previous year and enough to surpass the sport's previous record of 30.6 million, established in 2003 during the height of the Tiger phenomenon.

More than two decades after Woods helped transform golf into a mainstream sporting obsession, the game has reached another milestone. Only this time, it has done so under a very different set of circumstances.

The 1.7 million net increase represents the second-largest one-year gain in golf participation on record. Since 2019, before the pandemic fundamentally changed how Americans spent their leisure time, the number of on-course golfers has climbed by 6.5 million, a remarkable 27 percent increase.

Golf isn't simply recovering. It's expanding.

And the most interesting part of the story may be where people are playing. The golf landscape of 2026 looks considerably different from the one that existed in 2003.

Back then, the United States had more than 2,000 additional golf courses compared with today. The economy was strong, Tiger was dominating the sport, and social media hadn't yet become the all-consuming competitor for people's attention that it is now.

Golf had more places to play, but fewer ways to experience the game. Today, the sport is setting participation records despite having fewer traditional golf facilities and competing with an extraordinary range of entertainment options.

The game has also become more accessible in ways that would have been difficult to imagine during the original Tiger boom. You no longer need to reserve a tee time, find three playing partners or commit five hours to enjoy golf.

You can grab a bucket of balls at a driving range, rent a simulator bay with friends, visit a golf entertainment venue or work on your swing in your own garage. Golf has expanded beyond the fairways, and the numbers tell the story.

While traditional golf participation reached an all-time high, off-course golf established a record of its own.

An estimated 39.6 million Americans engaged with golf away from traditional courses in 2026, visiting driving ranges, indoor simulator facilities and golf entertainment venues.

This category has established a new participation record every year since the NGF began tracking it in 2014. Growth has moderated from the early years, largely because fewer large-scale golf entertainment venues have opened recently. But one segment continues to spread: golf simulators.

They're appearing in commercial entertainment facilities, country clubs, public golf courses, private homes and even garages. For some, they're a convenient way to practice. For others, they're an alternative to the traditional golf experience. And for an increasing number of people, they're simply a fun way to spend an evening with friends.

That audience barely existed during the 2003 participation peak. At the time, off-course golf largely meant hitting balls at a driving range. The NGF estimates that only 5 million to 6 million Americans participated exclusively in range-based golf. Today, the off-course universe is nearly eight times larger.

The definition of a golfer has also changed, and so has the business of golf. Perhaps the most revealing development is the growing number of people who participate in both versions of the game.

These are golfers who enjoy traditional green-grass golf but also participate in off-course golf activities. More than two-thirds of all on-course golfers now fall into this category. Their numbers have increased 42 percent since 2019 and 11 percent since 2024.

That's an important distinction because Dualies aren't simply casual visitors who occasionally pick up a club. They're among the most engaged participants in the sport. Compared with other golfers, they play more frequently and spend more money on the game. In other words, they're helping fuel both sides of the golf economy.

The traditional golf course remains the centerpiece of the sport, but the simulator, driving range and entertainment venue are increasingly becoming part of the same golf-centric lifestyle. And that's a significant shift for an industry that historically defined participation almost exclusively by rounds played on a golf course.

Add traditional and off-course participation together, and the numbers become even more impressive. A combined 49.5 million Americans participated in golf in 2026, another all-time high.

That's nearly 50 million people engaging with the game in one form or another. It's also a much broader audience than the one that existed during the Tiger Woods boom.

Some are dedicated players chasing lower handicaps. Others are occasional golfers who enjoy a weekend round. Some may never set foot on a traditional golf course, preferring the convenience and social atmosphere of a simulator or entertainment venue. But they're all part of the same expanding golf ecosystem.

For golf operators, equipment manufacturers, instructors, retailers and developers, that creates opportunities well beyond the traditional tee sheet. It also suggests that the future of the game may depend as much on attracting new participants to alternative golf experiences as it does on getting more people onto traditional courses.

The challenge will be converting that enthusiasm into long-term participation while keeping the game accessible, affordable and enjoyable.

There was a time when golf's growth seemed tied almost entirely to one extraordinary player. Tiger Woods inspired a generation, brought new attention to the sport and helped propel participation to record levels in 2003. Today, the game has reached an even higher peak without the same singular catalyst.

Instead, golf is benefiting from a combination of factors: increased interest in outdoor recreation, pandemic-era participation gains that have endured, technology, entertainment-driven venues and a broader definition of what it means to play the game.

The traditional round of golf isn't going anywhere. If anything, the record 30.8 million on-course participants demonstrate that its appeal remains remarkably strong.

But golf is no longer confined to 18 holes, a scorecard and a tee time. It's a driving range after work, a simulator on a rainy afternoon, a night out with friends or a weekend round with family. The game has found more ways to fit into people's lives, and millions of Americans have responded. Nearly 50 million participants later, golf has reached a new high-water mark.

The remarkable thing isn't just that the sport has broken its record. It's that there are now more ways than ever to be part of it.

Golf is booming again. And this time, the entire golf universe is along for the ride.

Adam Schupak is a senior writer for Golfweek, covering the PGA Tour.

articles.title: Jalen Green Trade Rumors Heat Up As Suns Reportedly Seek Proven Point Guard
articles.summary: The Suns are reportedly considering trading Jalen Green for a proven point guard amid his declining production.
articles.body:
Jalen Green scored 12 points against the Charlotte Hornets on Thursday, then watched the entire fourth quarter from the bench as Devin Booker closed out a 101–96 Phoenix Suns win. One rotation decision won't determine Green's future, but it captured how much his role has changed. The Suns once insisted Houston Rockets include him in the Kevin Durant trade. Now rival teams are wondering whether Phoenix would move him for a point guard.

According to Sam Amick of The Athletic , the belief around the league is that the Suns are motivated to swap Green for a proven floor general. A Phoenix source gave Amick a more measured account: The front office intends to give this roster time and may wait until later in the season before seriously engaging in trade talks.

"When Phoenix owner Mat Ishbia approved the Kevin Durant trade with Houston in the summer of 2025, it was because the Rockets had finally relented on the players that the Suns coveted. And Jalen Green, the No. 2 pick in the 2021 draft who was entering his fifth season at the time, was seen internally as a must-have part of the package."

"'It was never gonna get done without Jalen and Dillon (Brooks) in the deal,' Ishbia told me earlier this year. 'Those are the two players we wanted. It wasn't, 'Hey, how do we fill a salary with these numbers?' It was, 'In order to have Kevin Durant on your team, I want Dillon Brooks to help me with my culture and my identity. I want Jalen Green as a 23-year-old up-and-coming leading scorer.'"

"They landed Green, of course, but that last part about him heading up their offensive efforts has simply not come to bear for these Suns (5-6). After averaging 21 points per game in his final Rockets season, Green's scoring dipped to 17.8 in his first season with the Suns (in just 32 games) and currently stands at just 11.8 through his first 10 games (he's fourth in scoring behind Devin Booker, Miles Bridges and Brooks). In turn, there is a great deal of interest around the league in how Phoenix will handle Green (who has a player option worth $36 million for next season) heading into the deadline."

"The outside belief is that they are motivated to swap Green for a proven point guard. The Suns, according to a team source, insist that they'll remain patient with their roster and don't plan to truly engage in trade talks, potentially, until later in the season."

That's a notable shift from the summer of 2025, when owner Mat Ishbia saw Green as a player worth holding up the Durant deal for. Phoenix wanted Dillon Brooks to help establish its identity and Green to give it another young scorer capable of carrying an offense. The Suns got both, along with the draft rights to Khaman Maluach and five second-round picks.

Green averaged 21.0 points in his final season with Houston and 17.8 in his first year with Phoenix, when a hamstring injury limited him to 32 games. He's down to 11.8 points through 10 appearances this season, fourth on the team behind Devin Booker, Miles Bridges , and Dillon Brooks . He's also averaging 3.4 assists, and his $36 million player option for 2027–28 gives Phoenix another decision to weigh as the deadline approaches.

Chris Haynes reported in October that some Suns players were already frustrated by the lack of a traditional point guard. Booker can run the offense, but there's a difference between asking him to create an advantage against a set defense and getting him the ball after a teammate has already forced a rotation. An experienced lead guard could give Booker more catches on the move and get players like Maluach easier looks at the rim.

Dejounte Murray is one example of the kind of player who could help. Bleacher Report's Dan Favale floated a deal centered on Green and Murray , though that was a trade proposal rather than a report of negotiations. Murray's pick-and-roll passing addresses a clear need. His perimeter shooting and Achilles injury history also show why the Suns should be selective about what they give up for a veteran.

In the meantime, Jordan Ott can give Collin Gillespie more possessions alongside Booker and see how the offense looks with a dedicated organizer. Gillespie scored 13 points and hit three threes against Charlotte, a reminder that Phoenix has an internal option worth testing. Green is still 24, and moving him while his scoring is down could mean selling low.

If the Suns do trade him, the return should be someone they trust to run the offense in the fourth quarter, when Booker needs help most.

articles.title: Tiger Woods Pays Tribute to Dan Hicks, Commends Broadcaster's 'Lasting Impact' in New Statement
articles.summary: Legendary golfer Tiger Woods paid tribute to longtime broadcaster Dan Hicks, who died Thursday at the age of 64 after an acute illness.
articles.body:
Legendary golfer Tiger Woods paid tribute to longtime broadcaster Dan Hicks, who died Thursday at the age of 64 after an acute illness.

Woods commended Hicks for "the incredible job he did for our sport for decades," and he sent a message to broadcaster Hannah Storm and their children, saying, "I hope they find comfort in knowing how much he meant to so many people and the lasting impact he made on everyone whose life he touched."

Before the start of the afternoon round of the Austin Championship on Friday, the Golf Channel's Todd Lewis held a moment of silence to honor Hicks:

Hicks was the voice behind some of golf's most memorable moments, working as NBC's lead play-by-play announcer since 2000. He elevated Woods and many others through his words, and the golf world will not be the same without him.

articles.body:

articles.title: Erik Van Rooyen Says LIV Stars Must Re-Qualify
articles.summary: PGA Tour winner Erik Van Rooyen demands former LIV players earn their way back through Q-School, rejecting automatic reinstatement for stars like Jon Rahm.
articles.body:
Erik Van Rooyen said on Thursday that players who left for LIV Golf cannot simply walk back onto the PGA Tour. The South African golfer insists that former members must earn their spots through the standard qualifying process. During the Austin Championship, he started with a 64 that had no bogeys when he made those comments. While his ball-striking drew attention, his stance on tour rules sparked a bigger debate about fairness.

Van Rooyen believes the path back depends entirely on a player's current status. "I think it's completely status dependent, right? Like Jon Rahm has no reason to go back to Q-School," van Rooyen said Thursday. He argues that top stars might have other ways to return, but the rest must pay their dues. This view opposes the idea of a quick fix for the sport.

The 36-year-old pointed to his own career struggles to make his case. He started the 2026 season with nine straight missed cuts before finding his form again. Van Rooyen noted that if he had left for a different tour, he would lose his privileges. Returning would require him to work his way back up. "I have nothing against players that went to LIV, nothing personal at all," van Rooyen said. "But that's just how things work, right? So shouldn't we just follow the rules?"

This demand places him against those who want a fast track for ex-LIV players. The PGA Tour faces a tough choice as the rival league collapses. Some stars like Bryson DeChambeau and Tyrrell Hatton might need to rebuild their status from scratch. Van Rooyen's position ensures that the field remains competitive for everyone who stayed loyal.

The conversation extends beyond the United States. Peter Baker, a three-time European Tour winner, wants the DP World Tour to stop sending ten players to the PGA Tour every year. Baker told Golf Monthly that the current setup is flawed. "I certainly wouldn't be sending 10 of our best players over to America every year to play there, I think that needs to be looked at," he said, according to Yahoo . He believes the European circuit should be its own strong entity again.

Baker admitted the DP World Tour has struggled since LIV arrived. "It has been in a tricky spot for a while I think with LIV," he said. However, he sees a chance for the tour to grow now that the Saudi-backed league is fading. He wants the best players to stay home and support the European schedule rather than chasing money in America.

Van Rooyen is advocating changes to entry rules, while 91‑year‑old Gary Player is advocating the game itself. The Golfer's Journal was informed by Player that the golf ball needs an immediate rollback. He warned that modern power is destroying course design. "The game is changing against my better wishes," Player said, according to Yahoo Sports . He claims pros now hit drivers and eight-irons into par-5s, making old courses obsolete.

Player predicts the problem will get worse before it gets better. He stated, "Wait until the Michael Jordans and Shaq O'Neals come out and play golf. We haven't scratched the surface." He estimates that at least a trillion dollars is being wasted globally on course modifications to handle longer drives. The delay in implementing a ball rollback until 2030 has frustrated traditionalists who want immediate action.

Van Rooyen's stance on Q-School remains clear as the Austin Championship continues. He wants the standards to apply fairly to everyone, regardless of where they played last year.

articles.title: ‘Like Clockwork When (Stephen Curry) Is Out,’ ‘Pre-Eject Him in Some Games’ — Hoops Fans Blast Draymond Green Over Flagrant 1 on Victor Wembanyama
articles.summary: Draymond Green was assessed a Flagrant 1 after running through Victor Wembanyama from behind while the San Antonio Spurs star was trying to position himself...
articles.body:
Draymond Green was assessed a Flagrant 1 after running through Victor Wembanyama from behind while the San Antonio Spurs star was trying to position himself for an offensive rebound during Golden State's 123-85 loss Friday night.

The incident came during a game the home team controlled from the start. San Antonio opened a 26-5 lead, went up 38-14 after the first quarter and eventually led by as many as 43, while Green's foul drew plenty of reaction from fans.

Fans Troll Draymond Green After Flagrant 1 on Victor Wembanyama

Wembanyama finished with 12 points, 12 rebounds, 6 assists, and 2 blocks in 21 minutes as San Antonio improved to 11-2. The Spurs led from start to finish and held Golden State to 33% shooting.

Green's foul quickly drew attention online. Underdog NBA posted a clip of the play with the caption: "Draymond trucks Wemby. He was assessed a Flagrant 1."

Warriors Muse responded with a one-word question: "Why."

Golden State played without Stephen Curry, who suffered an oblique abdominal tear during Wednesday's 115-108 loss to the Houston Rockets. The Warriors announced Thursday that Curry will be reevaluated in two weeks.

Radio and podcast host Matt George tweeted : "Like clockwork when Steph is out."

NBC Sports Philadelphia's Tyrone Johnson added , "They should pre-eject him some games."

The Warriors forward had already been ejected once this month. Green received two technical fouls in quick succession during Golden State's 116-113 win over the Phoenix Suns on Nov. 2. The first came after he threw Khaman Maluach to the floor, while the second followed an ensuing confrontation with Dillon Brooks.

Some fans also questioned Green's actions on the play.

"He trying so hard to get ejected," one fan wrote .

One fan focused on Wembanyama's side of the incident: "Spurs need an enforcer like Isaiah Stewart 'cause they need to think twice before hitting Wemby."

The four-time NBA champion was not ejected against San Antonio. He finished with 4 points, 3 rebounds, and 3 assists in 16 minutes and did not play in the fourth quarter.

Golden State was missing several players in addition to Curry. Jimmy Butler, Moses Moody, Kristaps Porziņģis and Brandon Williams were also ruled out.

The Warriors never recovered from their slow start, scoring just 33 points in the first half and falling to 8-5. San Antonio extended its winning streak to 11 games, while Stephon Castle led all scorers with 32 points.

The flagrant became one of the lasting images from a night that quickly got away from Golden State.

articles.title: Anthony Kim Shares Emotional Update After LIV Golf Collapse
articles.summary: Anthony Kim has another uncertain chapter ahead of him, but his latest update offered a reminder that his comeback has always involved more than golf. With L...
articles.body:
Anthony Kim has another uncertain chapter ahead of him, but his latest update offered a reminder that his comeback has always involved more than golf. With LIV Golf shutting down, Kim is looking for somewhere to continue playing. However, the opportunity he received already helped him rebuild something more important than a professional career.

For fans, Kim's return meant seeing a familiar face after years away from competition. For Kim, getting outside and working toward a goal became part of his recovery.

That distinction matters when evaluating what his time with LIV meant. His explanation went beyond tournament results, money or the debate surrounding the league. He spoke about it in a post on his Instagram account.

"I've gotten quite a few questions about why I played on LIV and decided to take this opportunity," Kim said. "One, part of my rehab process was to be outside, and gave me a great opportunity to work on my sobriety while getting to do something I was once good at. For that, I'll always be grateful because sobriety, family, God, they're the most important things in my life."

There was something particularly revealing about how Kim described golf. He called it something he "was once good at," a modest assessment from someone whose talent once made him one of the sport's most compelling players.

His priorities, though, were clear. Golf gave him a place to put his energy. Sobriety and family gave that work a purpose beyond the scorecard.

Anthony Kim Explains What LIV Golf Meant to Him

Kim can appreciate what LIV provided while recognizing that the arrangement has reached its end. His gratitude does not solve the question of where he competes next, but it explains why he refuses to dismiss the experience.

"Being a part of LIV was something great for me at the time and I know, obviously, with LIV shutting down, I'm going to have to find a new path."

That new path comes with uncertainty. Professional golf does not guarantee a landing spot simply because a player has a recognizable name or a story people want to follow.

Kim now faces the challenge of keeping himself prepared without knowing when another invitation might arrive. That can make the daily work difficult. There is no confirmed destination in his comments, and no promise that the next opportunity will look like his last one.

However, Kim has already experienced how quickly circumstances can change. He pointed to that history while discussing the questions surrounding his future.

"I get a lot of questions of people asking what I'm doing next, but I do know that I'm going to keep working hard, stay ready. You never know when the opportunity is going to come because three years ago, I had no idea I was going to get phone calls to play professional golf again."

The phone calls changed his schedule and gave his golf another chance. They also became part of a recovery process that Kim now places above anything he might accomplish between the ropes.

Former LIV Winner Is Preparing for Another Opportunity

Kim's update did not include an announcement about a tour, tournament or contract. Instead, he offered a commitment to keep doing the work while those answers remain unsettled.

"I'm going to keep working hard, and I know an opportunity's coming, so just going to stay ready."

For someone whose return once seemed so unlikely, that belief carries weight. Kim does not need to know every detail of his future to find value in preparing for it.

His next scorecard remains a question. The priorities behind his comeback do not. Whatever opportunity comes next, Kim has already explained what he wants to protect most: his sobriety, his family and the life that made playing golf again possible.
